subject: mimicChest
pitch: A treasure chest that is not a treasure chest: the lid hinges open into a jaw of uneven fangs, a purple tongue lolls over the gold coins, little spidery legs prop it up, one eye peeks from the keyhole. Dungeons & Dragons manual illustration energy.
reasoning:
I'm designing a mimic creature module with a skeleton structure: a body root joint, a hinged jaw joint positioned at the back of the base that opens like a lid, and plans for additional limbs like a tongue.

I'm working out the exact dimensions and coordinate placement — base box height, lid curvature, hinge rotation direction — so the lid opens correctly when the jaw joint is posed with a positive rotation about the X axis.

I'll place lid parts in model-space coordinates attached to the jaw bone before posing, and set up the jaw joint hinge aimed along the z-axis with default roll so no local correction is needed. The mouth structure uses the lid as the upper jaw (bone jaw) and base as the lower jaw (body root), with the joint named "jaw" and role "jaw".

For materials, I'll use the clockwork kit's metal paints (gilt, iron) and the glow kit's glow paint rather than writing custom shaders, accepting the moderate risk that the kit import path resolves correctly since the spec documents it explicitly.

Writing wood paint logic...

For the actual geometry, I'm planning the base body as a tapered box using the wood paint, mounted on the body bone, with darker mottled tones toward the bottom and warmer tones up top based on normal direction, plus a dark interior cavity for the open top.

Adding fangs and rim details...

Now I'm figuring out the upper fangs on the lid, positioning them to point downward from the lid's underside so they interleave with the lower teeth when closed, and working out the lid geometry itself as a base slab plus a half-cylinder barrel top.

Still building the barrel arch geometry...

I'll settle on a general paint approach with seams driven by the normal direction—using y or z coordinates for sides and top, and angle-based seams for the barrel curve, accepting some discontinuity where these switch since it's stylized anyway. Then I'll add iron bands around the lid by extruding a slightly larger, thinner offset of the same arch shape.

Placing the bands at specific x positions on both lid and base, plus corner brackets with riveted detail using small boxes and spheres, keeping part count low by merging the rivet geometry.

For the gold coins, I'm piling tilted cylinder shapes near the interior floor spilling over the front lip where the tongue lolls, merging the varied tilted copies via matrix transforms with randomized positions in the mouth region.

Scattering a dozen or so extra coins around the feet on the floor near the tongue tip, and giving them two gilt color variants ('#f2c230' and darker '#d49a1c') for variety by merging a few differently colored groups.

I'm also adding textured coin faces on a handful of top-facing coins using a circle plane with an embossed gold-and-skull SVG texture, tilting some to vary orientation while keeping the rest as plain colored geometry.

Now I'm building the mouth interior: a flesh-colored floor slab beneath the chest, and a palate slab positioned just under the lid so it's visible when the lid opens, adjusting the box dimensions so the lid thickness and the palate underside align properly.

I could add a small dangling uvula sphere from the palate, optional detail. Now I'm plotting the tongue's curve as a chain of points, starting at the mouth floor, arcing up over the coins, draping over the front lip rim, and curling down the front of the mouth.

Shaping the tongue tube...

I'm adding papillae texture with lighter pink-purple spots, then giving the tongue a forked tip by branching into two small diverging capsule tips at the end of the main sweep. I'm also planning drooling slime strands hanging from the fangs as thin translucent green capsule shapes for extra character.

For the lock, I'm placing a gold keyhole plate on the front of the base, deciding the hasp should hang from the lid itself so it swings open naturally with a broken bone-jaw clasp detail.

Now I'm designing the keyhole itself with a bloodshot yellow eye peeking out—a black keyhole socket shape extruded slightly, with a partial eyeball sphere and slit pupil embedded just behind it for that classic mimic chest gag.

I'm texturing the eye sphere with a yellowish sclera covered in red veins, then adding eyelids as flattened, fleshy spheres scaled and positioned above and below to partially cover the eyeball, giving it that "peeking" look.

I'll simplify to full-sphere ellipsoids above and below the eye center instead of hemisphere domes, overlapping the upper and lower thirds. Then for the keyhole plate, I'm building the outline polygon combining a circular top with a trapezoid slot below, defining points around the shape to extrude as a black keyhole silhouette.

Still defining keyhole geometry...

I'm placing the eye to sink slightly into the keyhole so the black ring stays visible, with the pupil glancing toward the viewer and slightly left for a bit of horror flavor. For the legs, I'm deciding to go with 8 spidery legs propping up the body rather than 6.

For the leg structure itself, I'm working out an IK approach where each hip attaches near the underside of the base and the foot reaches outward and down, using three segments (femur, tibia, and a final joint) with knees bending upward and outward for that spider-like stance.

The limb returns four points giving three spans plus a tip joint, so I'm using tapering tube radii for a smooth segmented look, adding small iron claw cones at the feet and studs at the knees, with the foot targets sitting just above ground level.

I'm settling on legs colored as dark violet-brown chitin with pale joint bands for a spidery mimic feel, rather than iron or wood.

Adding joint rings...

I'm also considering small spikes along the femur and tibia of each leg, and planning z positions for the four leg pairs.

Positioning the hips so they embed slightly into the base's side walls, letting legs emerge naturally from the body, and spreading the foot targets outward with front legs sprawling a bit further forward than the chest line.

Checking that the lid, when opened to 55 degrees, doesn't collide with the legs or barrel top, and estimating the total height by tracking the hinge position, lid length, and rotated apex of the barrel lid.

Placing upper teeth rows along the lid front and sides with uneven lengths and the occasional oversized fang, then mirroring with lower teeth rooted in the base rim so they'd interleave when closed, varying radii and slight inward tilt for a jagged, chipped look.

I'm also adding fleshy "lip" strips along the rim edges beneath the teeth, using red-purple boxes to form a gum ring on both the upper lid and lower base so the teeth look rooted in flesh rather than floating on bare wood.

Still working out mouth geometry...

I'm working out a height profile for the coin heap and shaping the tongue's path so it emerges from the back of the mouth and rests just above the coins, adjusting its vertical position and thickness so the heap stays visibly tucked beneath it.

Still writing tongue path coordinates, checking where it curls down past the lip and tip, and watching for overlap with the eye and plate positions.

I realize the tongue would cross through the front row of teeth, so I need to skip teeth in that x range to avoid the clash. I'm also considering whether to add a small decorative hasp hanging off the lid's front, but I'm checking whether it would overlap with the lid's existing geometry before committing to it.

For positioning the hasp plate, I'm calculating where it sits along the arch's curved surface, solving for the angle and z-height so it sits flush against the lid front rather than floating off the surface.

Instead I'll use a nearest-surface hit on the lid to stick a small box for the hasp plate, oriented along the surface normal, plus a torus ring for the hasp loop — simpler than computing the curve manually, and it stays attached to the lid's bone correctly. I'll skip adding rivet rows via scatter for now to keep things simple.

For extra dungeon flavor I'm adding moss on the top wood faces, cracked and chipped wood details, nail heads, a coin heap with a ruby or emerald gem glow, and a small femur bone poking out as a lure detail — keeping it to just one eye per the prompt's constraints.

Giving the eye a subtle yellow glow, and considering corner iron brackets as L-shaped boxes around the base's vertical edges for extra structural detail.

Adding protruding corner posts, metal bands across the lid and base, and a darker skirt trim plate, then tallying up the piece count toward roughly 200 total elements.

Counting out the interior details next: hinges, hasp, keyhole, floor planks, teeth, coins, gems, bone, tongue with papillae, chained legs with spikes and studs, drool drips, and moss tufts scattered across the lid.

Totaling around 190 parts, I'm now planning the texture set: coin emblem, eye decal, moss tuft, glowing violet rune panels on the lid band for that classic mimic look, plus a skull emblem decal on the base sides and maybe a slime-drip texture.

I'm also setting up a weathered wood paint with darkened grain stains near the bottom and moss creeping up certain faces, using the SDK's shared noise and color utilities imported from the main package.

Still refining colors for flesh, teeth, and interior gradients, then starting on a coin-set generation function.

For the bone shape, I'm combining a capsule with knob spheres at the ends, colored off-white, and calculating its trajectory so it rests naturally over the lip rather than floating in space—tilting it downward slightly so it looks like it's drooping between the fangs instead of hovering awkwardly.

For the front teeth, I'm figuring out which x-positions to skip so there are visible gaps for missing teeth. For drool, I'm planning to sweep thin tapered strands downward from select upper teeth tips, giving them rounded caps and a small blob at the bottom, and making sure they're rigged to the jaw bone so they rotate naturally when the mouth moves.

Realizing the drool needs to be built after the pose is applied, using the posed tooth tip positions as frames, so the strands actually hang straight down in world space rather than rotating awkwardly with the jaw.

I need to build teeth sweeps before posing the jaw, since pose rotates all children in model space. Then after posing, I'll add the drool and other lid-mounted decorations like moss tufts scattered across the lid arch surface, using cards with slight lean and size variation bound to the jaw bone.

Thinking about scattering moss on the base too, but the top rim would be hidden under the lips and floor geometry, so cards there would just poke through. Better to skip moss on the base top and instead filter scatter hits to the sides and bottom edges where the normal points outward or downward, keeping the tufts visible near the base's lower rim.

Now writing the leg geometry: looping over left/right sides and four leg positions, computing hip and foot joint positions, then calling the limb function with segment lengths and a bend-direction hint to define the joint plane for the inner knee/ankle joints.

Checking the segment lengths against hip-to-foot distances for the front legs, it roughly works out.
